# A sharp mixed triangular/quadrilateral stationary-section subcase

This proves the exact γ_3 weighted inequality for a family containing
both orientations of a genuine quadrilateral section together with all
available vertex-isolating sections. The common section centroid has
two equal pairs of barycentric coordinates. No claim is made here for
arbitrary common centroids or all tetrahedral section patterns.

## Theorem

Let T be a tetrahedron and y an interior point with barycentric
coordinates (a,a,b,b), where a,b>0 and a+b=1/2. Consider the following
closed caps, each with boundary-section centroid y:

* both orientations of the quadrilateral section ξ_0+ξ_1=2a;
* both orientations of every vertex-isolating section with centroid y.

Give any finite collection of these caps nonnegative probability
weights θ_j. Write S_j for its section area, u_j for its unit inward
cap normal, and F_j for its volume fraction in T. If

    Σ_j θ_j S_j u_j=0,                                  (1)

then

    Σ_j θ_j F_j≥27/64.                                  (2)

The constant is sharp. It is attained at a=b=1/4 by the four
vertex-side caps with equal weights. If a quadrilateral cap has
positive weight, the inequality is strict.

All claims are affine invariant. We will divide section coarea masses
by |T| and use raw affine normals; their products equal S_j u_j/|T|,
so (1) is unchanged.

## 1. Cap fractions and normal vectors

Put U=∇(ξ_0+ξ_1), a nonzero continuous covector. For the quadrilateral
cap Q={ξ_0+ξ_1≥2a}, the marginal density of r=ξ_0+ξ_1 is
6r(1−r) on [0,1]. To verify this, fix r and use the two normalized
coordinates ξ_0/r and ξ_2/(1−r); the simplex-volume Jacobian is
r(1−r), and its integral over r is 1/6. Thus

    F_Q=1−12a²+16a³,
    q_Q:=S_Q u_Q/|T|=24ab U.                            (3)

Each section at fixed r is the product of its two pair segments, so
its centroid is (r/2,r/2,(1−r)/2,(1−r)/2), proving the required
centroid assertion at r=2a. Equivalently it follows from the exact
quadrilateral formulas with equal positive and equal negative vertex
values. The complementary cap has fraction 1−F_Q and vector −q_Q.

A vertex-side section with centroid y exists exactly when every
other barycentric coordinate is at most 1/3. Since each coordinate
occurs twice, either all four vertex sections exist or none exists.
If none exists, the only possible balanced caps are Q and its
complement with equal total weights, and their mean is 1/2.

Otherwise a,b≤1/3, equivalently a∈[1/6,1/3]. The vertex-side fractions
in the first and second pairs are

    F_A=27ab²,       F_B=27a²b.                         (4)

Use the raw vertex margins m_i=3−Σ_{j≠i}ξ_j/λ_j. Their normalized
coarea masses equal F_i, so their vectors are F_i∇m_i. Averaging
within each pair gives

    q_A=(q_0+q_1)/2=A U,
    A=(27/2)b(2a−b)≥0,
    q_B=(q_2+q_3)/2=−B U,
    B=(27/2)a(2b−a)≥0.                                 (5)

For example, ∇m_0+∇m_1=(2/b−1/a)U, which proves the first formula;
the second is the analogous identity. Set Q_0=24ab>0 for the positive
quadrilateral speed in (3).

## 2. Symmetry reduces the balance exactly to one dimension

Average the weights under the permutations of vertices 0,1 and of
vertices 2,3. These permutations fix y and Q, preserve cap fractions,
and permute the vertex caps. On the vector balance they act linearly
on barycentric covectors modulo constants, so averaging preserves
(1). It also preserves the weighted mean.

After averaging, each vertex-pair's total probability may therefore
be regarded as the probability of one type with fraction and vector
given in (4)–(5). There are three positive-normal types

    (A,F_A),  (B,1−F_B),  (Q_0,F_Q),

and three negative-normal types

    (A,1−F_A),  (B,F_B),  (Q_0,1−F_Q).

Here the displayed nonnegative speed is the magnitude of the
coefficient of U. A zero-speed type occurs only at a=1/6 or 1/3;
its fraction is exactly 1/2 and it may be handled separately.

Every scalar-balanced probability mixture of nonzero speeds is a
convex combination of mixtures of one positive and one negative
type. Here is an explicit proof. If positive types have probabilities
p_i and speeds s_i, and negative types probabilities r_j and speeds
t_j, their common flux is L=Σp_i s_i=Σr_j t_j. If L>0, couple their
fluxes by π_ij=(p_i s_i)(r_j t_j)/L. Assign probabilities π_ij/s_i
and π_ij/t_j to this pair. These allocations reproduce all original
probabilities and each pair is balanced. Its mean fraction is

    (t_j F_i+s_i G_j)/(s_i+t_j).                         (6)

If L=0, only zero-speed types are present and the mean is 1/2.

## 3. Enumerating the nine pair means

The three pairs of a cap type and its complement have mean 1/2.
The pair of A-vertex and B-vertex types has mean

    R_V=(B F_A+A F_B)/(A+B)
        =27a²b²/(1−6(a²+b²))≥27/64.                    (7)

The inequality is the already proved vertex-section product inequality;
it also follows by substituting (a,a,b,b) into that formula. Its reverse
pair has mean 1−R_V≥1/2, since R_V≤1/2.

The pair Q with the B-vertex type has mean

    f(a)=(B F_Q+Q_0 F_B)/(B+Q_0)
         =9(1−3a+4a³)/(17−43a).                        (8)

The pair of the A-vertex type with the complement of Q has mean f(b),
by exchanging the two equal pairs. Reversing these pairs gives
1−f(a) and 1−f(b). This exhausts all nine possibilities.

The formulas remain valid at the endpoints a=1/6 or 1/3; zero-speed
types have already been separated, and all remaining denominators in
(7)–(8) are positive.

## 4. An exact bound for every mixed pair

For x∈[1/6,1/3], the denominator 17−43x is positive. Direct algebra
gives

    1/2−f(x)
      =(1−3x)(24x²+8x−1)/(2(17−43x))≥0.                (9)

The quadratic is at least one on this interval. Also

    f(x)−4/9
      =(13−71x+324x³)/(9(17−43x))>0.                   (10)

For completeness, the numerator's global minimum on the nonnegative
axis occurs at x_*=sqrt(213)/54 and equals

    13−71sqrt(213)/81>0.

The last strict inequality follows by squaring positive quantities:
1053²−71²·213=35076>0. Thus

    4/9<f(x)≤1/2,
    1/2≤1−f(x)<5/9.                                   (11)

All mixed pairs therefore have mean strictly greater than 27/64.

Combining (6), (7), and (11) proves (2). Equality requires the
vertex-only mean at a=b=1/4 and zero contribution from every mixed
or complementary pair. In particular no quadrilateral cap may have
positive weight. This proves the stated sharpness and strictness.

## 5. Two further explicit quadrilateral plane types

When a∈(1/6,1/3), choose p,q>0 with

    p/q=(2−6a)/(6a−1).

The two additional raw plane value vectors

    (p,−p,q,−q),     (p,−p,−q,q)                       (12)

give sections with the same centroid (a,a,b,b). To verify this,
reorder the first plane's positive vertices as 0,2 and negative
vertices as 1,3. In the quadrilateral formulas from
`candidate d9c0dfe42c7f1e42`,
the parameters are then (p,q,p,q), for which α=δ=1/(4(p+q)).
Formula (2) in that note gives

    a=(p+2q)/(6(p+q)),   b=(2p+q)/(6(p+q)).

Swapping vertices 2,3 gives the second plane in (12). The simultaneous
swaps 0↔1 and 2↔3 negate either plane while preserving T, so each cap
fraction is exactly 1/2.

Both orientations of these two plane types may be added to the
theorem's allowed collection. Averaging under the same two independent
pair permutations makes their combined coarea-normal vector zero:
their raw barycentric normal vectors average to zero, and their
normalized coarea masses agree along the permutation orbit. Their
combined fraction is 1/2. Remove that balanced part; the remaining
mixture is the one already treated. Thus (2) remains valid with all
three explicit 2-versus-2 vertex partition types present, and positive
weight on any quadrilateral cap still forces strictness.

At a=1/6 or 1/3 the planes (12) degenerate to triangular sections;
the stated extension only concerns the open interval and does not
require a limiting classification.

## Scope

The theorem includes arbitrary nonnegative weights, either orientation
of every listed cap, and the edge cases in which a vertex section
passes through additional vertices. It does not classify all
quadrilateral sections with the same centroid; only the displayed
three plane types and their complements are included. It therefore
does not imply the unrestricted tetrahedral weighted-section theorem
or any mixed-integer depth bound.
